analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security's funding by applying its payroll tax to wages above $400,000.
analysis.headline: Sole-sponsored and referred to committee the day it was introduced, the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would keep Social Security payroll taxes on the first ~$142,800 of wages as under current law, then resume the tax on annual wages and self-employment income above $400,000. It would count those high earnings in the benefit formula at a modest 3 percent rate, and it would raise the income level at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $100,000, with the Treasury reimbursing the trust funds for that revenue loss.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries gain longer program solvency without benefit cuts. Retirees with total income between roughly the current thresholds and $100,000 would pay less federal income tax on their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security recipients and middle-income retirees

how_it_helps.text: Applies the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $400,000 per year, so the highest earners pay into the system beyond the current cap, extending trust fund revenue [S2][S3].

Counts earnings above $400,000 in the benefit formula at a 3 percent rate, so high earners who pay more also receive some additional benefit rather than paying into the system with no return [S2][S3].
Raises to $100,000 the income threshold at which a portion of Social Security benefits is included in taxable gross income, reducing the income tax burden on retirees with benefits [S2][S3].
Appropriates Treasury funds to replace the trust-fund revenue lost from the benefit-taxation change, holding Social Security funds whole [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with annual wages or self-employment income above $400,000 would pay Social Security payroll tax on that income for the first time. General taxpayers would cover the cost of reimbursing trust funds for the benefit-taxation cut.

drawbacks.text: The new payroll tax applies only above $400,000, leaving income between the current cap (~$142,800) and $400,000 untaxed — a 'donut hole' design that limits how much revenue the bill raises [S3].
Workers and self-employed people earning above $400,000 face a new tax on income that was previously exempt from Social Security payroll taxes [S2][S3].

Raising the benefits-taxation threshold to $100,000 reduces income tax revenue, and the bill covers that loss with a general Treasury appropriation rather than an offsetting cut, adding to general-fund costs [S3].
High earners would eventually receive larger benefits under the new 3 percent formula bracket, which slightly offsets the added revenue [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: high earners pay more, and Social Security's financing improves without cutting anyone's check. The design is imperfect — the donut hole between the current cap and $400,000 weakens the revenue gain, and the benefit-taxation relief is financed from the general fund rather than paid for — but the bill addresses a widely recognized long-term funding shortfall using the most progressive available lever.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Crist introduced the bill on April 1, 2021 [S1][S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor — the cosponsor list shows zero [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to its Subcommittee on Social Security on the day of introduction [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners who would have paid the new payroll tax on income above $400,000 are better off because the bill never advanced, and the existing Social Security financing structure remained unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Charlie Crist
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply Social Security payroll taxes to income above $400,000 and count those earnings in the benefit formula.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought Social Security payroll-tax expansion legislation to the House floor during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no party breakdown exists; a single House Democrat introduced it and no other member of either party signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Individuals earning over $400,000 in wages or self-employment income
industries.note: The bill would impose Social Security payroll taxes on their income above $400,000 for the first time, in exchange for a small 3 percent benefit credit. Their financial interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in extending program solvency.
They would pay less income tax on Social Security benefits, but the bill makes the trust funds whole with a general Treasury appropriation, shifting the cost to other taxpayers.
The hold-harmless appropriation for the benefit-taxation change is an open-ended draw on general revenue with no offsetting cut.
